title: Short Stuff: Andrew Jackson's Inauguration
summary: Short Stuff episode on Andrew Jackson's first inauguration on March 4, 1829, and the legend of the chaotic White House reception afterward. Josh and Chuck describe Jackson's populist appeal drawing crowds of common supporters to Washington, D.C. They contrast the account of Margaret Bayard Smith, whose letters to her daughter describe muddy boots, broken glassware, bloody noses and a Black Friday-like scramble for punch and cake, with historians' skepticism. Daniel Feller, editor of the Papers of Andrew Jackson, is cited as cautioning against taking the account at face value. The New York Spectator's colorful description is quoted, and Senator Daniel Webster's more restrained account is noted as omitting chaos. In 1978 the Tennessee Historical Society investigated; it called the scene sheer bedlam, while Senator James Hamilton of South Carolina called it a saturnalia but said most damage was minimal. The hosts conclude the truth likely lies between these accounts, with Webster the most reliable.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with brief banter about avoiding politics and introduce the topic of Andrew Jackson's first inauguration.

segments.title: Jackson's inauguration and populist crowds
segments.summary: Chuck introduces Jackson's March 4, 1829 inauguration and the tradition of open receptions at the White House. Josh describes the legend that ordinary supporters, drawn by Jackson's populism, overran Washington in celebration.

segments.title: Historians question the chaos account
segments.summary: The hosts note that historian Daniel Feller, editor of the papers of Andrew Jackson, cautions against the story's reliability, since much of it comes from Margaret Bayard Smith, a late-arriving Jackson opponent who wrote letters to her daughter.

segments.title: Bayard Smith's letters and the crowd estimate
segments.summary: Josh explains that Bayard Smith arrived after three o'clock because of large crowds, and that an estimated twenty thousand people attended the White House party. Chuck notes she called the crowd figure probably exaggerated.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: A short break in the conversation.

segments.title: Damage claims and Daniel Webster's account
segments.summary: Chuck describes reported bloody noses and thousands of dollars in broken glassware. He notes Senator Daniel Webster, also a Jackson critic, wrote about the day without mentioning chaos, describing people who had traveled five hundred miles to see General Jackson.

segments.title: Was the party a riot?
segments.summary: Josh argues Webster's silence suggests the disorder was minor or invented. Chuck suggests some wildness likely occurred, such as people standing on furniture. Josh describes Bayard Smith's portrayal of people scrambling for punch and cake as a Black Friday sale, and explains how the press amplified the story to satisfy opponents.

segments.title: New York Spectator's colorful description
segments.summary: Chuck reads a passage from the New York Spectator describing the crowd, including a dandy wishing he had no toes. The hosts joke about what the line means.

segments.title: Tennessee Historical Society's 1978 investigation
segments.summary: Josh describes a 1978 investigation by the Tennessee Historical Society, which called the scene sheer bedlam. It also cites Senator James Hamilton of South Carolina, a Jackson supporter who called it a saturnalia but said most damage was minimal. The hosts conclude the truth lies somewhere between, with Webster probably the most reliable.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck wrap up, calling it a fun story, followed by the show's production credit.
